sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Go's interface system is the foundation of testability. Any dependency (database, HTTP client, message broker) expressed as an interface can be replaced with a mock in unit tests and with a real implementation in integration tests. Interviewers ask about mocking to see if you design loosely-coupled code; they ask about integration testing to see if you can validate behaviour against real infrastructure without flaky tests.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Mock at the interface boundary, never at the concrete type. Define small interfaces close to where they are consumed (consumer-driven interfaces). Generate mocks with mockgen from the interface definition—never hand-write mocks for non-trivial interfaces. For integration tests, use testcontainers-go to start real Docker containers for Postgres, Redis, or Kafka inside TestMain; this eliminates test-environment drift. Use net/http/httptest for HTTP handler and client tests without a real server socket.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. gomock + mockgen: install mockgen, generate with //go:generate, use ctrl.NewController(t), mock.EXPECT().Method().Return(). 2. Interface-based mocking: small interfaces (1–3 methods), define interface in the consuming package, accept in constructor. 3. testcontainers-go: testcontainers.GenericContainer, wait.ForLog or wait.ForListeningPort, container.Terminate(ctx) in t.Cleanup. 4. httptest: httptest.NewServer wraps a Handler, httptest.NewRecorder for handler unit tests, inspect recorder.Body and recorder.Code. 5. Golden file testing: write expected output to .golden files, compare with -update flag to regenerate, stable for JSON/HTML output. 6. Integration vs. unit: unit is fast/isolated/uses mocks; integration is slower/realistic/uses real deps; run separately via build tags.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: • 'How do you mock a database in a Go unit test?' → define a Repository interface, generate mock with mockgen, inject via constructor. • 'Walk me through a testcontainers-go setup for a Postgres integration test.' → GenericContainer with postgres image, wait.ForListeningPort(5432), run migrations, inject DSN, Terminate in Cleanup. • 'When would you use httptest.NewServer vs. httptest.NewRecorder?' → NewRecorder for handler unit tests (no network); NewServer for client integration tests (real HTTP). • 'What is golden file testing and when is it appropriate?' → snapshot testing for complex outputs (JSON, HTML templates) where writing all assertions manually is impractical.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "I follow the rule: depend on interfaces, not concretions. When I write a service that talks to a database, I define a Repository interface with only the methods that service needs—usually three or four methods. I then run mockgen to generate the mock and use EXPECT chains in my unit tests to verify call sequences and return controlled errors. For integration tests I use testcontainers-go: in TestMain I start a Postgres container, run migrations with golang-migrate, and pass the real DSN to my repository. The integration tests run only when the 'integration' build tag is present, so they don't slow down the unit-test suite in development. For testing HTTP handlers I use httptest.NewRecorder to capture the response without opening a socket."
